extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers; readers of Montaigne and literary essays
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective Renaissance personal essay exploring self-knowledge, literary style, virtues, conduct, and social perception. The text mixes moral/philosophical prescriptions with observations on writing, speech, and bodily presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility about human knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The too good opinion that man has of himself is the nursing mother of all the most false opinions; curiosity of knowing things has been given to man for a scourge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts those who imagine great knowledge of external things (e.g., astronomy, the Nile) with their inability to know themselves: one should be skeptical of claims of grand knowledge when self-knowledge remains obscure. Examples: those who 'ride astride upon the epicycle of Mercury' who claim to see far into the heavens yet fail to understand themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modest self-judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: I look upon myself as one of the common sort... I have no better an opinion of myself; guilty of the meanest and most popular defects, but not disowning or excusing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approve of nothing in oneself lightly; the approbation of others should not inflate self-opinion. Montaigne ‘repudiates’ himself and feels his judgment tender and nice about himself—use self-criticism rather than self-conceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mediocrity in poets
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither men, nor gods, nor the pillars permit mediocrity in poets. (Horace: 'Mediocribus esse poetis...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry requires a high standard; mediocre composition in poets is especially intolerable. Montaigne wishes the sentiment enforced (e.g., 'written over the doors of all our printers') to forbid the entrance of many rhymesters. Example anecdote: Dionysius’s pompous verses provoked violent popular rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the overconfidence of bad poets
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Verum Nihil securius est malo poetae.’ — The truth is, that nothing is more confident than a bad poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad poets typically display excessive self-assurance; this overconfidence is a recognizable anti-pattern and often invites ridicule and harsh judgment (e.g., the story of Dionysius).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be critical when rereading your own work
rubrics_metrics.description: My works are so far from pleasing me, that as often as I review them, they disgust me: 'When I reperuse, I blush at what I have written...' (Ovid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that re-reading will reveal faults; maintain an internal ideal or 'disturbed image' of a better form than produced, and use that ideal to judge and revise. The existence of an unattainable ideal does not excuse not polishing the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depend on polish and grace to make writing pleasing
rubrics_metrics.description: All that pleases and infuses delight is due to the charming Graces; 'They abandon me throughout; all I write is rude; polish and beauty are wanting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 'handling adds nothing to the matter', then the subject must be forcible and full or the writer must work to secure polish and beauty. Avoid crude, unpolished delivery; cultivate the 'Graces' (elegance, charm) to make prose pleasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation but guard against obscurity from excessive brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: By endeavouring to avoid art and affectation I fall into the other inconvenience: 'Brevis esse laboro, Obscurus fio.' — Endeavouring to be brief, I become obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a trade-off: avoid artificial ornamentation, but do not compress language so much that meaning becomes obscure. Strive for a balance between naturalness and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow your natural voice but learn from masters
rubrics_metrics.description: I simply follow my own natural way; whence... it falls out that I am better at speaking than writing. Though I might imitate Seneca, Plutarch, Caesar, etc., I follow my own natural mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer authenticity of voice over slavish imitation; still, observe and learn from great writers who sometimes adopt popular modes supported by 'graces.' Imitation should inform, not replace, the writer's natural manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use motion, action, and performance to enliven discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion and action animate words... The comportment, the countenance; the voice, the robe, the place, will set off some things that of themselves would appear no better than prating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral performance elements (gesture, tone, presence, setting) can enhance persuasion and entertainment; recognize differences between speaking and writing and exploit performative resources when addressing audiences in person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language/idiom matters; regional speech can corrupt standard tongue
rubrics_metrics.description: My French tongue is corrupted... I never saw a man who was a native of any of the provinces... who had not a twang of his place of birth... There is, indeed... a sort of Gascon spoken, that I am mightily taken with: blunt, brief, significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that dialect and regional usage influence style and reception. Some local idioms (e.g., Gascon) may offer virtues (force, brevity) absent from 'graceful' standard speech. Choose registers appropriate to purpose and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body and appearance affect social authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is a thing of great recommendation... the beauty of stature is the only beauty of men... a graceful presence and a majestic mien beget authority; a leader's stature creates respect in followers and terror in the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the social capital of bodily presence: stature, bearing, and appearance influence leadership and reception. This is a pragmatic standard in social/political contexts rather than a moral endorsement of vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the whole person: reunite body and soul
rubrics_metrics.description: We must reunite and rejoin [body and soul]... to embrace, cherish, assist, govern, and advise [the body], and to bring it back and set it into the true way when it wanders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating body and soul as wholly separable; wisdom attends to both. Philosophical and religious traditions (Peripatetics, Christians) are cited to support attending to bodily as well as spiritual goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer truthfulness; abominate lying and dissimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: My soul naturally abominates lying, and hates the very thought of it... A man must not always tell all, for that were folly: but what a man says should be what he thinks, otherwise ’tis knavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value open speech and integrity: dissimulation breeds distrust and corruption. Exceptions exist (prudential omissions), but habitual lying or calculated dissembling is condemned and considered servile and cowardly. Authorities cited: Aristotle, Apollonius, Cicero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers and negotiators should keep faith for long-term advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: They often buy in the same market; they make more than one peace... Gain tempts to the first breach of faith... the first gain has infinite mischievous consequences... Soliman ordered the release of prisoners to avoid loss of future trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political prudence recommends keeping agreements: the short-term advantage of breaking faith is outweighed by long-term disrepute and inability to negotiate later. This is both an ethical and pragmatic standard for statesmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hazardous ambition; do not risk what suffices for uncertain advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Spem pretio non emo — I will not purchase hope at a price... I apply myself to what I see and to what I have in my hand... if a man have sufficient to maintain him... ’tis a great folly to hazard that upon the uncertainty of augmenting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer prudence and contentment with sufficiency over reckless pursuit of advancement. Excuse may exist (necessity) for young or dispossessed, but for those entrusted with family/honour it is folly to risk secure standing for uncertain gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contentment and moderation are virtuous and hard-won
rubrics_metrics.description: I had only need of what was sufficient to content me: which nevertheless is a government of soul... the virtue of moderation more rare than that of patience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate moderation and satisfaction with a modest condition; it is a challenging form of self-governance, often more difficult to achieve in abundance than in want. This is recommended as a life-goal rather than passive resignation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory is vital for judgment and public speaking; compensate when lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory is a faculty of wonderful use... for my part I have none at all... I could not receive a commission by word of mouth without a note-book... when I have a speech of consequence to make, if it be long, I am reduced to... getting by heart word for word what I am to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good memory supports complex speech and judgment; if one lacks memory, use practical compensations: notes, learning speeches verbatim ahead of time. This shapes how one prepares for oral tasks and commissions.
